title: Power & Identity
content_html:
Power and Identity in the Anthology

Four poems explore different forms of power: Percy Bysshe Shelley’s Ozymandias, William Blake’s London, Ted Hughes’s Hawk Roosting, and Philip Larkin’s Afternoons. Together they examine political tyranny, institutional oppression, natural dominance, and the quiet erosion of individual identity by time and domesticity.

Ozymandias — Percy Bysshe Shelley

Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Ozymandias in 1818 as a challenge to political power. The poem describes the ruined statue of an ancient Egyptian pharaoh lost in desert sand. Everything Ozymandias built has vanished — only the sculptor’s art and the boastful inscription survive, now bitterly ironic.

Key Fact

The inscription — “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” — was intended to intimidate rival kings with Ozymandias’s power. Now the “Works” have vanished entirely, and the boast becomes an unintentional warning: all political power is temporary. The dramatic irony is devastating.

Key quotations: “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert” — the statue is fragmented; the body (and power) destroyed. “Sneer of cold command” — harsh alliterative “c” sounds reflect the tyrant’s cruelty. “The lone and level sands stretch far away” — soft alliteration of “l” creates a vast, empty final image where nature dominates and human achievement has been erased completely.

London — William Blake

William Blake wrote London (1794) as part of his Songs of Experience. The speaker walks through London’s streets and sees suffering everywhere — caused not by nature but by institutions: the Church, the monarchy, and the economic system that creates poverty and exploitation.

Key Fact

Blake attacks three sources of power: the Church (“black’ning Church” appalled by the chimney-sweeper’s cry), the monarchy (“the hapless Soldiers sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls”), and the economic system that forces women into prostitution (“the youthful Harlots curse”). Each image links suffering directly to those in power.

Key quotations: “I wander thro’ each charter’d street” — “charter’d” means mapped and owned; even the streets and the Thames are controlled by commerce and power. “Marks of weakness, marks of woe” — repetition of “marks” suggests both visible signs and branding (as of ownership). “Mind-forg’d manacles” — the most powerful image: the chains are mental as well as physical, forged by acceptance of oppression as natural.

Blake uses synaesthesia and impossibility to create a nightmarish vision: blood running down palace walls, a church “black’ning.” The regular ABAB rhyme and ballad-like tetrameter create an ironic contrast between the poem’s musical form and its horrifying content — the pretty structure contains ugly truths, just as London’s wealthy façades hide exploitation.

Hawk Roosting — Ted Hughes

Ted Hughes wrote Hawk Roosting (1960) as a dramatic monologue spoken by a hawk. The bird describes its absolute dominance over its environment with chilling confidence: it sits atop the food chain, kills without remorse, and sees the entire world as existing to serve its needs.

Key quotations: “I sit in the top of the wood, my eyes closed” — the hawk is so powerful it does not even need to be alert. “I kill where I please because it is all mine” — the simplicity of the language mirrors the hawk’s unquestioning assumption of power. “No arguments assert my right” — power here needs no justification; it simply exists. “Nothing has changed since I began. / My eye has permitted no change” — the hawk presents itself as controlling time and nature itself.

The poem can be read as nature poetry — an accurate portrayal of a predator’s instinctive confidence. But many readers interpret it as a political allegory: the hawk’s voice resembles that of a dictator who believes power is natural and permanent (“I am going to keep things like this”). Hughes denied the political reading, but the ambiguity enriches the poem. Either way, the speaker’s absolute certainty and lack of self-doubt are what make the poem disturbing.

Afternoons — Philip Larkin

Philip Larkin wrote Afternoons (1959), observing young mothers in a park as their children play. The poem quietly documents how motherhood and domesticity have eroded the women’s individual identities — their lives have been absorbed into their families’ needs.

Key quotations: “Summer is fading” — literal season change, but also metaphorical: their youth is fading. “Their beauty has thickened” — a delicate, almost kind observation that nevertheless acknowledges physical change. “Something is pushing them / To the side of their own lives” — the passive construction and vague “something” suggest forces the women cannot name or resist. Identity is eroded not by tyranny but by the quiet accumulation of domestic responsibility.

Key Fact

Larkin presents a different kind of power loss: not through tyranny or violence, but through the gradual, invisible pressure of domesticity and time. The women have not been oppressed by a tyrant — they have been displaced from their own lives by the roles of wife and mother. The poem raises questions about whether this is natural, chosen, or socially imposed.

Types of power: Ozymandias represents political tyranny (now fallen). Blake exposes institutional oppression (ongoing). Hughes depicts natural/absolute power (unchallengeable). Larkin shows power’s quiet erosion of identity (invisible).

The speaker’s position: Shelley uses a framing narrative (distance). Blake walks through the city (witness). Hughes speaks as the powerful figure (dramatic monologue). Larkin observes from outside (detached observer).

Tone: Shelley is ironic, Blake is angry, Hughes is coldly confident, Larkin is melancholy. These different tones shape how each poet communicates their message about power.
exam_tip_html: When comparing poems about power, be specific about what kind of power is being explored. Political tyranny (Ozymandias), institutional oppression (London), natural dominance (Hawk Roosting), and domestic displacement (Afternoons) are all “power” but work very differently. The strongest responses compare not just the theme but the methods: how does each poet’s choice of speaker, imagery, and form shape the reader’s understanding of power?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shelley uses dramatic irony and a ruined statue to show political power is temporary; Blake uses synecdoche and sensory imagery to expose ongoing institutional oppression.
  • Hughes’s dramatic monologue presents power as natural and absolute; Larkin observes its quiet erosion of women’s identity through domesticity.
  • Comparing these poems effectively means identifying different types of power and analysing how form and imagery communicate each poet’s attitude.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Shelley in 'Ozymandias' and Blake in 'London' present the abuse of power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Contrasts Shelley's fallen ancient tyrant with Blake's present-day institutional oppression. Analyses how irony (Shelley) and synaesthetic imagery (Blake) create different effects. Both are Romantic radicals but use different approaches.

Secure: Clear comparison with analysed quotations.

Developing: Some comparison with relevant references.

Emerging: Simple statements about each poem.

practice_questions.text: How does Hughes present power in 'Hawk Roosting'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses the dramatic monologue form, the hawk's absolute certainty, and the simple declarative language. Explores both nature and political readings. Discusses how lack of doubt makes the voice disturbing.

Secure: Clear analysis of key quotations with explained effects.

Developing: Some relevant comments with textual support.

Emerging: Basic description of what the hawk says.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Hughes in 'Hawk Roosting' and Larkin in 'Afternoons' present different relationships with power.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Contrasts the hawk's absolute possession of power with the women's gradual loss of it. Analyses how dramatic monologue (confident) differs from third-person observation (melancholy). Both present power as 'natural' but from opposite ends.

Secure: Clear comparison with analysis of methods.

Developing: Some comparison with references.

Emerging: Simple identification of differences.

practice_questions.text: How does Blake use imagery to criticise institutions in 'London'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses 'mind-forg'd manacles' (mental oppression), 'black'ning Church' (moral failure), blood on palace walls (state violence). Discusses how regular form creates ironic contrast with content.

Secure: Clear analysis of images linked to institutions.

Developing: Some relevant comments on imagery.

Emerging: Basic identification of criticism.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Shelley in 'Ozymandias' and Hughes in 'Hawk Roosting' present powerful figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Contrasts the fallen power (Ozymandias's boast now ironic) with the hawk's present-tense absolute control. Shelley uses framing narrative for distance; Hughes uses first-person for immediacy. Different messages: power falls vs power endures.

Secure: Clear comparison with language analysis.

Developing: Some comparison with references.

Emerging: Simple statements about both.

practice_questions.text: How does Larkin present the loss of identity in 'Afternoons'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses 'Something is pushing them to the side of their own lives' — vague agent, passive construction. Discusses seasonal metaphor, 'thickened' beauty, and the wedding albums 'near the television.' Links to 1950s gender expectations.

Secure: Clear analysis with explained effects.

Developing: Some relevant comments.

Emerging: Basic description of the poem's content.

glossary_terms.definition: Romantic poet (1792–1822) and political radical who challenged tyranny, religion, and social convention.
Romantic poet and artist (1757–1827) who attacked social injustice, the Church, and political oppression.
Poet Laureate (1930–1998) known for powerful poems about the natural world and animal kingdom.
Movement poet (1922–1985) known for precise, observational verse about ordinary English life.
When the audience understands the full significance of words or events that a character does not.
A poem in which a character (not the poet) speaks, revealing their personality through their words.
Mixing different sensory experiences in description, such as describing sounds in terms of colour.
A narrative in which characters and events represent abstract ideas or moral qualities beyond the literal story.
A figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or the whole represents a part.
A regular rhythmic pattern (often alternating tetrameter and trimeter) associated with traditional storytelling verse.
